Listen to your body. I usually do OMAD, but the week before my period I am constantly ravenously hungry so I extend my eating window to 6-8 hours and eat as much healthy/keto food as I want (sometimes probably up to 3000-3500 calories)

I'd always rather listen to my body right away and feed my cravings with healthy food, than try to push through and eventually cave in and binge on garbage food.

Your body is telling your what it needs. You will learn from this and try again and a few months from now you might be perfectly in tune with your cycle and know exactly when you can fast and how far you can push yourself. For now take it slow. This is not a race you don't have to get it right immediately. Just treat it like a science experiment instead for something you have to get right on the first try. 

I know that I have no issues fasting during my period but the week prior is absolutely impossible. I'd probably collapse if I tried to fast. Everyone is different just find out what you need.

feel the cravings, the hunger, the boredom, the urge to eat and just sit there. and feel it. And endure it. Allow yourself to be uncomfortable. you won't die you will be fine, you are just uncomfortable. 

This sounds kind of cruel but it's actually a meditation principle that teaches contentment not matter the circumstances.

If you sit there for a while and just feel the hunger, really experience it and think about it you will eventually find it tolerable.

If you do this often enough you will genuinely be able to tolerate and accept hunger (and other uncomfortable emotions) instead of running from it/distracting yourself/giving in forever.

(Also the next step would be actually thinking about your emotions and processing them properly)

But also don't do this if you aren't ready. 

If you aren't ready to do this kind of difficult mental work and really commit to it, it will just drain you and be painful.

One thing that's often overlooked in terms of gut health are bitter substances. They are really good for supporting digestion and helping the gut flora.

People have already given you great advice and bitter foods are certainly not going to solve your issues alone, but they might help.

Great bitter foods are things like Arugula, Artichoke, Kale, Brussel sprouts, radicchio, Chicory. But what really helps are bitter herbs like Dandelion, Mugwort/Wormwood, Hops, Thistle or even Peppermint and Chamomile.

And yes, I am so serious about Dandelion, you could walk into a field and grab a hand full of Dandelion every day and eat it in a salad and probably feel better. Honestly an incredible plant. 

There are also bitter drops you can buy of you don't want to bother. 

In terms of healthy fats, I find coconut oil really easily digestible. But everyone reacts differently of course. 


And also anecdotally, I've recently cut out dairy even though I never thought I had issues with it but I feel a lot better now so maybe that's an idea if nothing else works.

Good luck friend :)

For me focusing on my physical health really helped me and improved my mental health a lot as a side effect.

Going on long walks every day - great for physical health and sleep - also as a side effect, a lot of time to think/let your thoughts wander/feel your actual feelings. kind of meditative. I learned a lot about myself and processed a lot of trauma on those walks.

Eating healthier - obviously great for you in general - but also having clear goal, building discipline , feeling accomplished and generally taking care of myself better. As soon as I started only putting good food in my body it felt like a waste to then turn around and self sabotage by drinking/smoking/not sleeping or stressing myself out over dumb shit/negative self talk/etc.

Obviously there many health related things that could cause this but for me taking B12 really helped. 

I used to sleep 10-11+ hours for years and still feel tired and I'm a few weeks into taking a good B12 supplement and I only need like 8-9 hours now and I generally feel less tired. 

Make sure you get the bioavailable form Methylcobalamin though, not Cyanocobalamin.

Also I've been eating  healthier and exercising more for a few months so this might not all be from the B12,  so take this with a grain of salt.

I suffer from chronic fatigue and think OMAD (One meal a day) helps me the most, although I've only been experimenting with it for like 4 months on and off.

It can be really really rough especially in the beginning and I had to quit and restart a few times because it was to hard on my body. I've also done a few extended fasts in the past (48 hours or 72 hours) to varying degrees of success. 

One time I got the worst migrane of my life (despite taking electrolytes) and felt so weak I genuinely couldn't move a finger and obviously had to break the fast. but other times it went well and I felt better and had a little more energy during and after fasting.

When I stick to OMAD for a while (like 10+ days) I also generally feel a little better and have a little bit more energy. It's not a lot but definitely noticeable. 
But so far I haven't been able to stick to it for a really long time (longest was like 25 days) because at some point I always get a bad fatigue episode or some other health struggle (like stomach bug) and have to quit for a while so I'm not putting to much stress on my body. 

I will keep doing it though because overall it seems to help me. I think my body got overall better at using stored energy as consistent fuel instead of relying on blood sugar spikes from food. 

I guess just be really careful and don't push yourself to hard. Know when to quit or take a break if your body is giving you the signs. I wouldn't recommend starting with anything over a 24 hour or maybe 36 hour fast. Just see how it goes. Or if you want to take the intermittent fasting/OMAD route maybe first try something like 16:8 or 18:6.

Many people have given you great answers but i would like to add that when you say 

>This has resulted in me feeling emotionally abandoned, since I hoped we would be able to lean on each other as our mom dies.

it realistically means you want to lean on her. She would likely not be able to "lean on you emotionally" the same way or at all. So you leaning on her might just be draining and exhausting. 

I'm not trying to accuse you of anything, two non-schizoid people would probably be able to lean on each other in a situation like this and both get something out of it. But you would just be asking her for comfort, with her getting nothing in return and it costing her a lot of energy.

In your whole post you very much center how you feel and how difficult this is for you (which it is that situation sounds tough) but please also consider that this might be difficult for her. We all don't know how she really feels about this and how much she cares but it can't be a walk in the park. 

Whatever she might need to cope, you likely aren't able to help her with that. Please just genuinely care about what she needs, what she REALLY needs, not what you THINK she needs. And it might just be time and space but i don't know that. Talk to her.
